newsitem.title: CANADA: MOTOR RACING-SCHUMACHER WINS AFTER PANIS CRASH ENDS RACE.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-SCHUMACHER WINS AFTER PANIS CRASH ENDS RACE.

text.p: Twice world champion Michael Schumacher regained the lead in the drivers' championship when he was declared the winner of the crash-hit Canadian Grand Prix on Sunday.

The Ferrari driver was two seconds ahead of second-placed Jean Alesi after 54 laps of the scheduled 69-lap race when it was halted because of a massive accident involving Alesi's fellow Frenchman Olivier Panis.
Panis, in a Prost car, crashed after 51 laps at high speed into the barriers, wrecking the front end of his vehicle.

He was lifted from the cockpit and taken by stretcher to the circuit medical centre before being taken by helicopter to hospital. The race continued behind a safety car for three laps before being stopped.
Early reports at the circuit said Panis had suffered a broken right leg and a suspected broken right arm. He was said to be conscious and in a stable condition.

Victory lifted Schumacher to 37 points in the drivers' championship, seven clear of nearest rival Jacques Villeneuve of Canada who crashed out in front of his home fans on the second lap. But the German refused to celebrate his win.
"This is not a real win and there is nothing to celebrate. I am more concerned about Olivier after his accident," Schumacher said.
He also admitted he was a lucky winner because Briton David Coulthard had been 30 seconds ahead of him when he pitted in his McLaren shortly before Panis's accident.

Unfortunately, for Coulthard, he stalled in the pit lane and after rejoining the race was down in seventh place and out of the points. "If he had not had his problem, he would have been the winner," admitted Schumacher.
Italian Giancarlo Fisichella recorded the best result of his career to take third place for Jordan ahead of German Heinz-Harald Frentzen in a Williams.
Briton Johnny Herbert was fifth for Sauber and Shinji Nakano of Japan scored the first point of his career by finishing sixth in the second Prost car.
The race had only 10 finishers from 22 starters but these included world champion Damon Hill of Britain who reached the end for the first time this season in his Arrows Yamaha car.
Although the race ran for 55 laps, the result officially was declared after 54 laps.
The accidents and the drama meant that Coulthard and McLaren's fine, but flawed, performance was overshadowed.
The victory was the 24th of Schumacher's career and his second this season.
At the start, the double world champion catapulted his car into an instant lead from his 15th pole position.

Behind him, Giancarlo Fisichella jumped from sixth to third in his Jordan Peugeot. The leaders filed through the opening long right-hander safely but in the midfield scramble Panis ran into Eddie Irvine's Ferrari.
The Ulsterman, so luckless in similar circumstances in Melbourne's opening race, spun out. Panis survived, pitted for a new nose and continued his eventful and painful race.
It was always expected to be a race of attrition -- only eight finished in 1996 -- but no-one could have envisaged Villeneuve's mistake and retirement on lap two.
He approached the final chicane too quickly and, on his own admission, lost control of his car which slewed into the barriers.
The local hero, as stunned as the spectators, banged his gloved fists against his helmet in frustration as he walked away. "It was my own fault," he confessed.
This left Schumacher's Ferrari in a relatively comfortable leading position, with Fisichella chasing before Ukyo Katayama crashed heavily in his Minardi Hart.

This accident required a recovery truck on track and therefore a safety car before racing resumed on lap 10. Four laps later Ralf Schumacher's Jordan plunged off-circuit and speared into a tyre-wall at the entry to the Senna curve.
It was a major accident but the 21-year-old German walked away unhurt just as his brother began a spell of coruscating laps.

When Fisichella and Alesi pitted together, the Benetton crew sending their man out in front after 25 laps, Schumacher led by 10 seconds and followed them in for a swift 7.8 seconds blur of scarlet activity. It was impressive stuff and Coulthard led by only 9.9 seconds when Schumacher resumed.
The Briton, on a one-stop strategy, stayed in front for 12 laps before pitting himself. This gave Schumacher the advantage again, but only for four laps until he pitted again with blistered tyres.
Coulthard swept through, his McLaren looking poised and fast, to lead by 12 seconds while the field behind stretched and broke up under the strain.
It looked easy for Coulthard but his smooth progress was upset when he stalled, after pitting for new tyres, and the outcome was the chaotic finale in which Panis was carried from his wrecked car.
